title: The good news is you can change your label. Here's how: 📍 Pick one thing you want to be known for and say it the same way everywhere, in person, in your bio and in your DMs. If it…
caption:
The good news is you can change your label. Here's how:

📍 Pick one thing you want to be known for and say it the same way everywhere, in person, in your bio and in your DMs. If it keeps changing, people won't remember any of it.

📍 If your friend said something vague like "he's a cool guy," that's what you need to fix. Nobody gets introduced for being cool.

📍 Show it right there in the conversation. If you're the Instagram guy, fix their bio on the spot. Seeing it sticks way better than hearing about it.

📍 Say it again when you leave, something like "Good meeting you, if you know any coaches send them my way." People tend to remember the last thing you said.

caption:
Try it this week. Here’s what you need:

Questions that make the test work:
📍 “What got you into this?”
📍 “What are you working on right now?”
📍 “How do you know the host?”

Stay away from yes or no questions. Nobody can ask you something back after “Yeah.”

If they pass, go one level deeper. Ask why they picked that, or what’s been hard about it. That’s when people start remembering you.

If they don’t, here are two easy ways out:
📍 “I’ll let you get back to it, really good meeting you.”
📍 “I’m gonna grab a drink, catch you later.”

caption:
You've got your Intro Line. Here's how to make it land:

→ Make the pain specific enough to see. "Struggling with marketing" is vague. "Empty classes on weekdays" is something they can picture.

→ Use the same line everywhere: your IG bio, your LinkedIn headline, your first DM. People start repeating it for you.

→ When someone says "oh, I know a guy," ask them right there: "Would you be cool introducing us?" Most intros die because nobody asks.

→ Test it on a friend. If they can't name one person who fits, your "who" is too broad.

"You need money to start a business."
"I'd push back a little. You need money to grow, you're right. But your first client can come from one conversation."

Two rules. Push back on small opinions, never on someone's work or values. And only do it when you actually disagree, because fake pushback is easy to spot.

📍 "You went full-time freelance. Should I quit now or wait for 3 clients?"
📍 "You grew your page without ads. Start on LinkedIn or Instagram?"

title: The loudest person in the room is usually the least confident one. Before you comment "my friend is loud and super confident": I'm not talking about people who are just naturally…
caption:
The loudest person in the room is usually the least confident one.

Before you comment "my friend is loud and super confident": I'm not talking about people who are just naturally expressive. Some people are loud because that's their energy, and they're fine being quiet too.

I'm talking about the guy who NEEDS to be heard. He talks over people, repeats his point until someone agrees, and gets uncomfortable the second the room stops looking at him. That's the performative leader.

Here's the full breakdown of what certain people do instead:

1. They lower their voice when they want attention. The room leans in to hear them.
2. They say it once. Repeating yourself tells people you don't think it landed.
3. They don't end with "right?" or "does that make sense?" Asking for agreement makes it sound like you need it.
4. They're okay with silence. After they make a point, they stop talking and let it sit, even when it feels awkward.
5. They don't compete for the room. When someone else is talking, they actually listen.

Try one of these in your next meeting and watch how people react.

Be honest: have you ever been the loud one? 

Send this to the loudest person you know.

title: Logic won't get you a yes, and the research backs this up. In a 1999 study, researchers Davis and Knowles sold holiday cards door to door. When they said "They're 300 pennies... t…
caption:
Logic won't get you a yes, and the research backs this up.

In a 1999 study, researchers Davis and Knowles sold holiday cards door to door. When they said "They're 300 pennies... that's $3. It's a bargain," sales nearly doubled compared to just saying "$3." Same cards. Same price. No better reason.

Here's why it works. When someone asks you for something, your brain starts building resistance before they finish talking. I call it the No Reflex. Researchers call this technique disrupt-then-reframe. A slightly odd phrase (the disrupt) jams that reflex for a moment, and a clear reason delivered right after it (the reframe) lands before the resistance comes back.

That's the 300 Pennies Formula:
→ Focus: get their attention first. Eye contact, their name.
→ Interrupt: say the ask in a slightly unexpected way.
→ Suggest: give the reason immediately, while their brain is catching up.

The order matters. If there's a gap between the weird part and the reason, the No Reflex comes back.

3 ways to use it:

1 Asking a favor
"Got 180 seconds? That's three minutes. Quick, I promise."

2️⃣ Pricing your offer
"It's $1.64 a day... that's $50 a month. Less than one dinner out."

3️⃣ Pitching an idea at work
"What if we cut 50% of our meetings? That's every other one. Same work, way more time."

One honest note: this works best for small, reasonable requests. It helps a good offer land. It won't save a bad one.

title: Your best trait is shaping how people see everything else about you, whether you know it or not. That's the Halo Effect: a mental shortcut where one positive quality, like looks,…
caption:
Your best trait is shaping how people see everything else about you, whether you know it or not.

That's the Halo Effect: a mental shortcut where one positive quality, like looks, confidence, or warmth, makes people assume you're better at everything else too. Smarter, more trustworthy, more capable, without any real evidence.

Psychologist Edward Thorndike named it in 1920. He noticed that military officers who rated a soldier highly on one trait tended to rate him highly on all the others. Since then, researchers have found it in job interviews, classrooms, and even courtrooms.

Most people think it's only about being attractive. But in a 1977 study by Nisbett and Wilson, students rated the same professor's appearance, mannerisms, and accent as more appealing just because he acted warm instead of cold. And they had no idea it was influencing them.

You can't change your face, but you can change your first 30 seconds:
→ Smile before you speak
→ Use their name early
→ Ask about them before talking about yourself

caption:
**The weirdest part about getting what you want? Sometimes, getting it kills the excitement.**

You finally get the car. The relationship. The money. The achievement.

So why does something you wanted for months suddenly feel… normal?

Two psychological concepts help explain it:

**Anticipatory pleasure** — the excitement we experience while imagining and looking forward to a future reward.

And **hedonic adaptation** — the tendency for the emotional impact of a positive experience to diminish as we become accustomed to it.

While you're chasing something, your brain gets to keep imagining the reward.

Once you have it, the uncertainty disappears.

And after experiencing it repeatedly, what once felt extraordinary can become your new normal.

So sometimes, you aren't craving the thing itself.

You're craving the **feeling of getting closer to it.**

But here's the part that's even more interesting:

**If the excitement fades once we get what we want, why do we immediately start wanting something else?**

That's where the real pattern begins.
